Thought I would take a crack at this, as it was a good exercise for me as well. Here's my take, which include some adaptations I've made for my own trading: 1) First FTR: Validly identified. However I look for the RBR that every DBR reacts to (The DBR in this case being your FTR). This RBR was not engulfed where you marked, so I wouldn't consider the next level an FTR. And the RBR bounced price nicely to the next supply on this timeframe. 2) If you follow/agree with the logic of #1, then the 2nd FTR marked is not an actual FTR. And it also seems as part of a compression, so I wouldnt look to trade it, nor would I look for an engulf of the level to ID the next FTR. 3) 3rd FTR identified not valid as per my rules because of statements in #2. But when the compression is broken a little higher, I see a nice FL created which bounces price a couple of times in that flag (above where you marked your 3rd ftr). Thats a nice trade. Also looking to the right, when that FL breaks, looks like a new FL is formed and a nice bounce from it when revisited. 4) Your fourth FTR would not be an FTR, even if the first 3 were valid, because a lower low was not made. 5) Because of #4, your 5th FTR was not valid. It really is a pain in the A because if you identify one thing wrong, it can lead to a series of incorrect levels. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2345-mm-s-journal 10/37 7/27/2018 MM's Journal - RTM Community Also - assuming all were identified correctly, it also pays to look at the quality of the HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT level. So each FTR is pretty much a RBD or DBR. Look at each on your timeframe, and see which of these you see a clear drop, basing, then rally (or vice versa). It's really only the 3rd FTR which could meet this criteria. Alot of them CP into or out of the base which isnt great. And the 3rd one likely didnt react because it wasnt actually an FTR. Hope this helps! This is just my take, though. Would love to hear others' input. Also consider that I am still figuring things out, so I may not be 100% right, but what I explained is my current understanding, and I'm currently applying it with some degree of consistency. But I am not yet a profitable trader, and still on demo. So use what I said as an idea for your research, not fact. With that said - forgetting all I said about "IDing the RBR that the FTR reacted to", etc... The FTR setup starts with "some important barrier" being engulfed to start off the process. For me, identifying this barrier regularly is my main challenge. But with that in mind, the first high you were looking at (I assume) which was engulfed and caused the first FTR you marked.. those highs were part of a compression as far as I can see. So I would consider the important barrier to be the high of the compression. In which case there was no FTR. Again - focus on ID'ing which barriers are important (compression, FTR, FL, etc), and then begin looking for an FTR. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2345-mm-s-journal 14/37 7/27/2018 MM's Journal - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Just my two cents! QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU MM's Journal #375 dengaima Offline Trader Posts: 370 Thank you received: 319 3rd last arrow from the right is demand and the second from the right is ignored demand. See how if marked the box? He marked between decisions and high = PAZ. Also where you marked other arrows on the left looks like CP. Ignored levels are always respected sooner or later. Reason = Demand becomes Supply and vice versa. Also they are fresh levels once they break something significant. In this case I think it broke flag limit. I noticed how you mark the levels thinking they are fresh in your journey.. I suggest u to check HTF to see if they are really fresh levels. And then finally I'm looking further left to find the LS that matches with my DP to identify my entry. If I marked every significant higher or low on my chart, the chart would soon be unreadable. So it seems more logical to find these last to me. Thought I would take a crack at this, as it was a good exercise for me as well. Here's my take, which include some adaptations I've made for my own trading: 1) First FTR: Validly identified. However I look for the RBR that every DBR reacts to (The DBR in this case being your FTR). This RBR was not engulfed where you marked, so I wouldn't consider the next level an FTR. And the RBR bounced price nicely to the next supply on this timeframe. 2) If you follow/agree with the logic of #1, then the 2nd FTR marked is not an actual FTR. And it also seems as part of a compression, so I wouldnt look to trade it, nor would I look for an engulf of the level to ID the next FTR. 3) 3rd FTR identified not valid as per my rules because of statements in #2. But when the compression is broken a little higher, I see a nice FL created which bounces price a couple of times in that flag (above where you marked your 3rd ftr). Thats a nice trade. Also looking to the right, when that FL breaks, looks like a new FL is formed and a nice bounce from it when revisited. 4) Your fourth FTR would not be an FTR, even if the first 3 were valid, because a lower low was not made. 5) Because of #4, your 5th FTR was not valid. It really is a pain in the A because if you identify one thing wrong, it can lead to a series of incorrect levels. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2345-mm-s-journal 10/37 7/27/2018 MM's Journal - RTM Community Also - assuming all were identified correctly, it also pays to look at the quality of the HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT level. So each FTR is pretty much a RBD or DBR. Look at each on your timeframe, and see which of these you see a clear drop, basing, then rally (or vice versa). It's really only the 3rd FTR which could meet this criteria. Alot of them CP into or out of the base which isnt great. And the 3rd one likely didnt react because it wasnt actually an FTR. Hope this helps! This is just my take, though. Would love to hear others' input. Can anybody help me out??? https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2345-mm-s-journal 9/37 7/27/2018 MM's Journal - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT These are just some FTR's I have marked out of what I see, what on earth am I missing??? Thought I would take a crack at this, as it was a good exercise for me as well. Here's my take, which include some adaptations I've made for my own trading: 1) First FTR: Validly identified. However I look for the RBR that every DBR reacts to (The DBR in this case being your FTR). This RBR was not engulfed where you marked, so I wouldn't consider the next level an FTR. And the RBR bounced price nicely to the next supply on this timeframe. 2) If you follow/agree with the logic of #1, then the 2nd FTR marked is not an actual FTR. And it also seems as part of a compression, so I wouldnt look to trade it, nor would I look for an engulf of the level to ID the next FTR. 3) 3rd FTR identified not valid as per my rules because of statements in #2. But when the compression is broken a little higher, I see a nice FL created which bounces price a couple of times in that flag (above where you marked your 3rd ftr). Thats a nice trade. Also looking to the right, when that FL breaks, looks like a new FL is formed and a nice bounce from it when revisited. 4) Your fourth FTR would not be an FTR, even if the first 3 were valid, because a lower low was not made. 5) Because of #4, your 5th FTR was not valid. So each FTR is pretty much a RBD or DBR. Look at each on your timeframe, and see which of these you see a clear drop, basing, then rally (or vice versa). It's really only the 3rd FTR which could meet this criteria. Alot of them CP into or out of the base which isnt great. And the 3rd one likely didnt react because it wasnt actually an FTR. All the best MM !! Thought I would take a crack at this, as it was a good exercise for me as well. Here's my take, which include some adaptations I've made for my own trading: 1) First FTR: Validly identified. However I look for the RBR that every DBR reacts to (The DBR in this case being your FTR). This RBR was not engulfed where you marked, so I wouldn't consider the next level an FTR. And the RBR bounced price nicely to the next supply on this timeframe. 2) If you follow/agree with the logic of #1, then the 2nd FTR marked is not an actual FTR. And it also seems as part of a compression, so I wouldnt look to trade it, nor would I look for an engulf of the level to ID the next FTR. 3) 3rd FTR identified not valid as per my rules because of statements in #2. But when the compression is broken a little higher, I see a nice FL created which bounces price a couple of times in that flag (above where you marked your 3rd ftr). Thats a nice trade. Also looking to the right, when that FL breaks, looks like a new FL is formed and a nice bounce from it when revisited. 4) Your fourth FTR would not be an FTR, even if the first 3 were valid, because a lower low was not made. 5) Because of #4, your 5th FTR was not valid. It really is a pain in the A because if you identify one thing wrong, it can lead to a series of incorrect levels. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2345-mm-s-journal 10/37 7/27/2018 MM's Journal - RTM Community Also - assuming all were identified correctly, it also pays to look at the quality of the HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT level. So each FTR is pretty much a RBD or DBR. Look at each on your timeframe, and see which of these you see a clear drop, basing, then rally (or vice versa). It's really only the 3rd FTR which could meet this criteria. Alot of them CP into or out of the base which isnt great. And the 3rd one likely didnt react because it wasnt actually an FTR. Hope this helps! This is just my take, though. Would love to hear others' input. With that said - forgetting all I said about "IDing the RBR that the FTR reacted to", etc... The FTR setup starts with "some important barrier" being engulfed to start off the process. For me, identifying this barrier regularly is my main challenge. But with that in mind, the first high you were looking at (I assume) which was engulfed and caused the first FTR you marked.. those highs were part of a compression as far as I can see. So I would consider the important barrier to be the high of the compression. In which case there was no FTR. So it seems more logical to find these last to me.
